title: Test Coverage
body:
Choosing which inputs to test. [[Unit testing]] in [[INTRODUCTION TO SOFTWARE ENGINEERING]] owns
the practice of testing a function in isolation, and [[Driver]] is the harness that runs it; this
note is about the question those two do not answer, which is **which values**.

You cannot try them all. Even `def add(a, b)` over two integers has more input pairs than there
are atoms in anything. So testing is sampling, and the whole skill is sampling on purpose rather
than by habit.

## Categories, then boundaries

**Partition the input space into classes where you expect the code to behave the same way, then
test one value from each class plus every value on a class edge.**

For `def grade(mark)` returning a letter for a mark out of 100:

| Class | Test with | Why |
|---|---|---|
| typical pass | 75 | the ordinary case |
| typical fail | 40 | the other ordinary case |
| **boundaries** | 49, 50, 59, 60 | every threshold, and the value either side of it |
| edges of valid | 0, 100 | the ends of the range |
| invalid | -1, 101, `"abc"` | what should it do? Decide, then test it |

**The boundary row is where the bugs are.** `>` against `>=` is the most common
[[Logic Errors|logic error]] in a first course, and it is invisible at 75 and obvious at 50. Off-by-one in a loop is the
same mistake wearing a hat; see [[Tracing Table]] and [[Control variable]].

The invalid row is the one people skip, and in [[Python]] it is the one that bites, because
nothing checks types until the line runs. A function that is never tested with a bad input is a
function whose behaviour on bad input is unknown, not correct.

## Test as you go, not at the end

Block 6's "validating functions independently" is the actual instruction: write a function, test
that function, then write the next one. A program tested only once it is finished gives you a
wrong answer and a hundred lines of suspects. [[debugging]] is what you are trying to avoid
needing.

The limit is worth knowing early, because [[INTRODUCTION TO SOFTWARE ENGINEERING]] states it
formally: **testing shows the presence of bugs, never their absence.** Only a [[Proof]] covers
the whole input space, and almost nothing is proved.
